items.prompt: Which is the largest bird alive?

options.label: The ostrich
options.feedback: Up to 2.8 m tall and 150 kg, and it cannot fly.

options.label: The emu
options.feedback: Second in size, and a good deal lighter.

options.label: The cassowary
options.feedback: Heavy and dangerous, but shorter than an ostrich.

options.label: The wandering albatross
options.feedback: The widest wings of any bird, and a modest body.

items.ok_line: The biggest bird on Earth has not flown for millions of years.
items.ko_line: The largest wingspan and the largest body belong to different birds.
items.exp_text: An ostrich stands up to 2.8 m and weighs as much as two adults. Flight has a ceiling: past roughly 15 kg the wing area and muscle needed grow faster than a body can supply, which is why the heaviest fliers — bustards and swans — sit near that mark. The ostrich abandoned the air entirely and spent the savings on legs, ending up with the largest eye of any land animal, wider than its own brain.

items.prompt: What is missing from the chest of a flightless bird?

options.label: The keel
options.feedback: No keel means nothing for flight muscles to grip.

options.label: The wishbone
options.feedback: Many flightless birds keep one.

options.label: The lower ribs
options.feedback: Every bird has ribs, flying or not.

options.label: The air sacs
options.feedback: They serve breathing, and they remain.

items.ok_line: No pull, no ridge. The bone follows the muscle.
items.ko_line: Think about which bone existed only to anchor the flight muscles.
items.exp_title: A bone that vanished with its job
items.exp_text: The keel is a blade of bone down the breastbone that the flight muscles grip. Where flight is abandoned those muscles waste, nothing pulls on the keel, and it flattens away — the ostrich, emu, rhea and kiwi all have a smooth breastbone, and the group is named for it. Penguins are the exception that proves the rule: they cannot fly in air but fly hard underwater, so their keel is enormous.

items.prompt: How does a penguin move underwater?

options.label: It flies with its wings
options.feedback: The same stroke as a bird in air, in a denser medium.

options.label: It paddles with its feet
options.feedback: The feet steer, like a rudder. They do not drive.

options.label: It beats its tail like a fish
options.feedback: A penguin's tail is short and stiff.

options.label: It rides the current and glides
options.feedback: A hunting penguin turns faster than any current.

items.ok_line: It never stopped flying. It changed the medium.
items.ko_line: Watch one underwater and it looks exactly like a bird in the air.
items.exp_text: A penguin beats its stiff flat wings in the same figure-of-eight a flying bird uses, and gets thrust on both the down and up strokes. Water is some 800 times denser than air, so the wings are short, solid and blade-like rather than broad. The bones are dense instead of hollow, since buoyancy is the enemy here. An emperor penguin dives beyond 500 m and stays under for more than twenty minutes.

items.prompt: Why did so many island birds lose the ability to fly?

options.label: There was nothing to escape from
options.feedback: No ground predators, and flight is expensive to maintain.

options.label: The islands were too small to fly across
options.feedback: Birds cross whole oceans to reach islands.

options.label: The sea air damaged their feathers
options.feedback: Seabirds fly through salt spray their whole lives.

options.label: There was too little food to fuel flight
options.feedback: Islands they colonised were often rich in food.

items.ok_line: Flight is costly. Remove the reason for it and it goes.
items.ko_line: Ask what flying is mostly *for*, on the ground, day to day.
items.exp_text: Flight muscles can be a fifth of a bird's weight and demand constant food. On islands with no mammals, birds that flew less survived as well as those that flew more, and over generations the wings shrank. It has happened again and again — rails alone have lost flight on dozens of islands independently. The trap closed when people arrived with rats, cats and pigs: a bird that cannot run and cannot fly has nothing left.

items.prompt: What was the dodo's closest relative?

options.label: The pigeon
options.feedback: A giant flightless pigeon of Mauritius.

options.label: The ostrich
options.feedback: Flightless too, but from a quite separate line.

options.label: The turkey
options.feedback: Its build misled early naturalists into thinking so.

options.label: The penguin
options.feedback: Nothing links them beyond being unable to fly.

items.ok_line: A pigeon that landed on an island and grew.
items.ko_line: Its nearest living cousin is a bird you might see on any city square.
items.exp_title: A pigeon that outgrew the air
items.exp_text: DNA from museum specimens placed the dodo firmly among the pigeons, its nearest living relative the Nicobar pigeon of South-East Asia. Its ancestors flew to Mauritius, found no predators, and over time grew large and lost flight — the island pattern exactly. It disappeared within about a century of sailors arriving, killed less by hunting than by the rats and pigs that ate its ground-laid eggs.

items.prompt: Which flightless bird is considered the most dangerous?

options.label: The cassowary
options.feedback: A dagger claw on each inner toe, and it will use them.

options.label: The emu
options.feedback: Large and fast, but it prefers to run.

options.label: The rhea
options.feedback: Nervous and shy, and it flees.

options.label: The kakapo
options.feedback: A heavy, gentle, nocturnal parrot.

items.ok_line: A kick from one can open a person from chest to knee.
items.ko_line: The bird is from the rainforests of New Guinea and Queensland.
items.exp_text: A southern cassowary stands up to 1.8 m, weighs around 60 kg and carries a claw on each inner toe reaching 12 cm. It kicks forwards and downwards, and the wound can be fatal. On its head is a tall horny casque whose purpose is still argued — display, pushing through undergrowth, or a resonator for the deep boom it makes, a call so low it is felt as much as heard. The male incubates the eggs and raises the chicks alone.

items.prompt: What is unusual about a kiwi's nostrils?

options.label: They are at the tip of its beak
options.feedback: It sniffs out worms underground, unlike almost any bird.

options.label: It has four of them
options.feedback: Two, as in every other bird.

options.label: They close completely underwater
options.feedback: A kiwi does not swim or dive.

options.label: They are hidden under feathers
options.feedback: That would defeat the point of having them there.

items.ok_line: The only bird with its nose at the far end of its beak.
items.ko_line: The bird hunts underground in the dark. What does it need at the beak's tip?
items.exp_title: A bird that hunts by smell
items.exp_text: Almost every bird has its nostrils at the base of the beak; the kiwi has them at the very tip, and probes leaf litter sniffing for worms and grubs. It is nocturnal, its eyes are tiny and poor, and its sense of smell is exceptional for a bird. Its feathers are loose and hair-like, it has whiskers around the face, and its body temperature runs several degrees below other birds — closer to a mammal's.

items.prompt: How fast can an ostrich run?

options.label: About 70 km/h
options.feedback: The fastest of any two-legged animal alive.

options.label: About 25 km/h
options.feedback: Barely faster than a person, and easily caught.

options.label: About 40 km/h
options.feedback: Quick, but well short of what it manages.

options.label: About 120 km/h
options.feedback: No running animal on land reaches that.

items.ok_line: Faster than any other creature running on two legs.
items.ko_line: It outruns a racehorse over distance. Aim higher.
items.exp_text: An ostrich sprints at around 70 km/h and holds 50 for half an hour, outlasting a horse. Its stride reaches five metres. It has two toes where most birds have four, the inner one enlarged into something close to a hoof, and its leg tendons store and return energy at each step like a spring. It still uses the wings — spread as air brakes and as a rudder in a turn taken at speed.

items.prompt: Which is the smallest flightless bird?

options.label: The Inaccessible Island rail
options.feedback: About 35 g, on one small island in the Atlantic.

options.label: The little spotted kiwi
options.feedback: The smallest kiwi still weighs over a kilo.

options.label: The kakapo, a ground parrot
options.feedback: The heaviest parrot alive, up to 4 kg.

options.label: The little blue penguin
options.feedback: About 1 kg, and small only among penguins.

items.ok_line: Thirty-five grams, and its whole world is one island.
items.ko_line: It is a rail, and it lives on an island whose name says how hard it is to reach.
items.exp_title: A whole species on one island
items.exp_text: The Inaccessible Island rail weighs about 35 g — roughly a house sparrow — and lives nowhere but a single island in the South Atlantic, some 14 square kilometres of it. Its ancestors flew there from South America and lost flight, as rails so often do. It survives only because the island is genuinely hard to land on: no rats or cats have ever reached it, which is the whole of the reason it still exists.

items.prompt: What does a kakapo do that no other parrot does?

options.label: It booms at night from a hollow
options.feedback: A low call carrying kilometres, from a scooped bowl of earth.

options.label: It hunts small animals
options.feedback: It eats leaves, seeds and fruit.

options.label: It builds a nest of woven grass
options.feedback: It nests in hollows and burrows, unwoven.

options.label: It migrates each winter
options.feedback: It can barely walk a hillside, let alone migrate.

items.ok_line: The only parrot that cannot fly, and the only one that booms.
items.ko_line: The clue is in how a bird that cannot fly reaches a mate across a valley.
items.exp_text: The kakapo is the world's only flightless parrot, nocturnal and up to 4 kg. Males dig a bowl in the earth, positioned to throw sound outward, and boom into it through an inflated chest for hours a night, for months — a note so low it carries several kilometres. Females walk in from far off. They breed only in years when certain trees fruit heavily, which is part of why fewer than 250 birds remain.
